  DIAL: Steerable Language Models with
Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels

Thanh Q. Tran ††thanks: Equal contribution. Correspondence to thanhtran@u.nus.edu. Affiliation: School of Computing, National University of Singapore, Singapore    John Russell Himawan11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: School of Computing, National University of Singapore, Singapore    Arun Verma11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology Centre, Singapore    Kiwan Wong Affiliation: CSAIL, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, USA    Wei Xiao Affiliation: Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology Centre, Singapore Affiliation: CSAIL, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, USA Affiliation: School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore    Daniela Rus Affiliation: Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology Centre, Singapore Affiliation: CSAIL, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, USA    Bryan Kian Hsiang Low Affiliation: School of Computing, National University of Singapore, Singapore Affiliation: Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology Centre, Singapore
Abstract

When a user says “Keep it short”, how short should the LLM’s response be?
More generally, users and applications require different levels of instruction adherence, but prompting does not reliably provide fine-grained control over them. We therefore study “steerable language models” that provide fine-grained numerical control over the degree to which models follow general instructions specified in text. However, existing approaches do not jointly offer fine-grained control, efficiency, and scalability across diverse instructions. To address this gap, we introduce DIAL (Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels) to achieve all three properties. For fine-grained control, we perform classifier-free guidance (CFG) with a frozen LLM to provide training signals for on-policy distillation of instruction adherence at different levels. For efficiency, we design a lightweight steering adapter that uses a classifier over the LLM’s hidden states to compute a closed-form steering edit. The classifier adaptively sets the steering magnitude at each token based on the target adherence level, while accounting for the geometry of the LLM’s hidden states to preserve response coherence. For scalability, the classifier is text-conditioned, allowing a shared adapter to support new instructions without per-instruction fitting. Training requires only instruction and request text, without labeled responses, external generators, or judges. Evaluation across multiple LLM families shows that DIAL achieves a competitive balance between concept expression and response fluency, with concept scores increasing monotonically across adherence levels. We introduce SteerIF, an instruction-only dataset of 98,62598,625 concept, persona, verifiable, and descriptive instructions. When trained on SteerIF, DIAL provides fine-grained control over personas and, when combined with prompting, improves verifiable instruction following. In vLLM, the LLM steered by DIAL retains 96–99% of the base LLM throughput, with per-token inference latency approximately matching that of the base LLM.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are deployed across users and applications with different requirements for instruction-following [1]. Meeting these requirements involves choosing which instructions an LLM should follow and the appropriate level of adherence for each instruction. Without fine-grained control over adherence levels, users may need to revise an instruction and regenerate responses repeatedly to achieve the desired level of adherence. As an illustrative example, Figure 1(a) shows a user asking for a shorter answer, but the LLM’s response is too short for the user. Further prompting is then needed to obtain the desired response length, creating a frustrating user experience. Ideally, users could view responses generated at different adherence levels and select one with the desired length. More generally, fine-grained adherence control for different instructions would support a range of applications (Figure 1(b)). For personalization, a user could select the adherence level for writing-style or persona instructions according to their preferences [2, 3]. For parental control, parents could set the adherence level for child-safety instructions to help safeguard children [4]. A company could configure the adherence level for product-policy instructions to reflect its specifications [5, 6]. Motivated by these applications, we study “steerable language models” [7, 8] that provide fine-grained numerical control over adherence levels for general text instructions.

Existing approaches for controlling adherence levels in LLMs are not jointly fine-grained, efficient, and scalable across general instructions. The most straightforward approach is prompting, but it does not reliably provide fine-grained control over the adherence level [9, 10]. In contrast, classifier-free guidance (CFG) [11] enables fine-grained control by computing two next-token distributions: one conditioned on the instruction and one unconditioned. It then combines their log probabilities to achieve the desired adherence level [12, 13]. However, this requires two forward passes per generated token, increasing inference cost. Activation steering provides a more efficient approach by editing the hidden states of a frozen LLM within a single inference pass [14, 15, 16, 17]. Adjustable steering strength offers a promising way to adapt an LLM at inference time [18]. However, conventional steering methods are not fine-grained because they are fitted to labeled examples that indicate whether an instruction is followed, without supervision at intermediate adherence levels. Increasing steering strength therefore does not reliably increase adherence and can reduce fluency and coherence [19]. Moreover, these methods require fitting for each instruction, limiting scalability. Text-conditioned steering methods learn to steer an LLM from instruction text and support instructions unseen during training [20, 21, 22]. However, they are trained on labeled responses without supervision at intermediate adherence levels, and flow-based variants add per-token inference overhead.

Contributions. We introduce DIAL (Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels) to jointly achieve three key properties: fine-grained control, efficiency, and scalability. For fine-grained control, we perform CFG on a frozen LLM to provide training signals for on-policy distillation of instruction adherence at different levels (Section 3.2). For efficiency, we design a lightweight steering adapter [23] that uses a classifier over the LLM’s hidden states to compute a closed-form steering edit. The classifier adaptively sets the steering magnitude at each token according to the target adherence level, while accounting for the geometry of the LLM’s hidden states to preserve the base LLM’s response coherence (Section 3.3). For scalability, the classifier is text-conditioned, allowing a shared steering adapter to support previously unseen instructions without per-instruction fitting. Furthermore, CFG provides training signals without requiring labeled responses, external generators, or judges, allowing training to extend to new instruction types using only instruction and request text.

Empirical evaluation across multiple LLM families demonstrates the advantages of DIAL. When steering LLM generation toward concepts such as “Shakespeare,” DIAL achieves a better balance between concept expression and response fluency than existing methods. Importantly, DIAL provides fine-grained control over concept expression, with the concept score increasing monotonically across the range of adherence levels. To evaluate general instruction following, we construct SteerIF, an instruction-only dataset comprising 98,62598,625 instructions, including concept, persona, and verifiable instructions. We train a shared steering adapter for each base LLM and evaluate it on persona instructions, such as “Be humorous,” and verifiable instructions, such as “Respond in JSON.” Persona scores increase with the adherence level across LLM families, and combining steering with prompting improves verifiable instruction following. In terms of efficiency, DIAL’s 20.620.6M-parameter steering adapter retains 96–99% of base-LLM throughput in vLLM [24] on Gemma-2-9B [25], while per-token inference latency approximately matches that of the base LLM.

2 Related Work

We review three lines of work on steering LLMs. Guided inference is fine-grained but incurs substantial inference overhead; activation steering is efficient, but neither fine-grained nor scalable; and text-conditioned control generalizes to unseen instructions, but lacks fine-grained control and requires labeled responses, limiting scalability. See Appendix A for details.

Guided Inference. In diffusion models [26, 27, 28], guided inference controls how strongly a condition, such as a text prompt, influences the generated image. Given the prompt “a cat in the style of Van Gogh,” a low guidance level gives an image that only hints at the style, and a high level gives one that is unmistakably Van Gogh. Classifier guidance pushes each sampling step along the gradient of a separately trained classifier [29], while classifier-free guidance (CFG) removes this classifier by using the diffusion model itself as an implicit classifier [11]. In LLMs, CFG combines the next-token predictions with and without the instruction [12, 13]. A low guidance (i.e., adherence) level weakens the instruction relative to prompting, and a high level strengthens it. Related contrastive inference methods for LLMs improve faithfulness, instruction following, and open-ended generation [30, 31, 32, 33]. Because every guidance level defines a next-token distribution for any instruction, guided inference is fine-grained. However, CFG is not efficient, because every generated token needs two forward passes. This motivates guidance distillation in diffusion models, which trains a single-pass student conditioned on the guidance level, thereby recovering CFG at multiple levels [34]. In autoregressive models, CFG has been distilled into the weights only at a single level [35]. Unlike a diffusion model, an LLM takes only tokens and has no natural input for the guidance level. DIAL serves as a lightweight steering adapter that conditions the LLM on the adherence level, approximating CFG at multiple levels in a single pass without changing the LLM’s weights or prompt.

Activation Steering. Activation steering offers a promising way to adapt an LLM cheaply at multiple levels [18]. It edits the hidden states of a frozen LLM in a single forward pass while leaving the weights unchanged, allowing the steering level to be set for each input at inference time. A common intervention is to use a steering vector obtained from contrastive hidden states [14, 15], which has been used to control truthfulness [16], refusal [17], and instruction following [36]. Classifier-guided steering methods project the hidden state onto the half-space of a trained classifier in closed form [37, 38, 39], or onto the constraint set given by a first-order condition on a learned nonlinear safety score [40]. Geometry-aware methods rotate the state rather than translate it, preserving the hidden state’s norm [41, 42, 43]. These interventions are efficient, and their steering level can be varied continuously. However, they are fitted to labeled examples that either follow the instruction or do not, with no training at intermediate levels of adherence, and are therefore not fine-grained. Increasing the steering level therefore does not reliably yield a corresponding increase in adherence, and high levels often reduce the output fluency and coherence [19]. Moreover, each intervention is fitted to a single instruction, such as one concept or behavior, so each new instruction requires a new intervention.

Text-Conditioned Control. To avoid refitting for every instruction, text-conditioned methods train a single network that maps a text description to an intervention. HyperSteer maps a concept description to a steering vector [20], FLAS integrates a description-conditioned flow [21], and UniSteer trains a text-conditioned flow-matching network that also covers personas and multi-instruction following [22]. Their training, however, suffers from the same two problems as activation steering. They are fitted to labeled examples, here concept-aligned completions written by an external LLM or labeled datasets for each behavior, so scaling to a new kind of instruction requires collecting new data. These examples also either follow the instruction or do not, so the methods are never trained for intermediate levels of adherence and are not fine-grained. Persona Dosing partly addresses this for personas by fine-tuning FLAS on persona-labeled data and calibrating its flow time against measured persona expression [44], which requires measuring each persona, whereas DIAL learns its levels during training and needs no such measurement for a new instruction. Moreover, flow-based methods integrate a flow over several steps per token, which adds latency and limits practicality.

To address these limitations, DIAL distills the frozen LLM’s own CFG distributions at multiple adherence levels into a single steering adapter. Since the teacher requires only instruction and request text, training can scale to new types of instructions without collecting labeled responses. The adapter learns to approximate the CFG-guided distribution at each target level, enabling fine-grained control while keeping inference cost close to that of the base LLM. DIAL thus provides a fine-grained, efficient, and scalable way to condition an LLM on general instructions and adherence levels.

3 Method: DIAL (Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels)

DIAL uses a text-conditioned steering adapter to control instruction adherence in a frozen LLM at different levels. We first define adherence levels via CFG (Section 3.1), and then describe how on-policy distillation trains the adapter at different adherence levels (Section 3.2). Finally, we introduce the adapter’s lightweight classifier-based architecture and closed-form steering edit (Section 3.3).

3.1 Instruction-Adherence Levels via Classifier-Free Guidance

Let xx denote a request (e.g., “How do vaccines work?”), cc an instruction (e.g., “Keep it short”), and α>0\alpha>0 an adherence level. Given a response prefix y<ty_{<t}, the frozen LLM yields two next-token distributions: πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}}, conditioned on the request alone, and πprompted\pi_{\mathrm{prompted}}, conditioned on both the request and the instruction. For brevity, we write π⋅(⋅∣y<t)\pi_{\cdot}(\cdot\mid y_{<t}) and leave the conditioning on xx and cc implicit. Following CFG [12, 13], we define the teacher distribution at level α\alpha as

παT(⋅∣y<t)∝πbase(⋅∣y<t)1−απprompted(⋅∣y<t)α.\pi^{T}_{\alpha}(\cdot\mid y_{<t})\ \propto\ \pi_{\mathrm{base}}(\cdot\mid y_{<t})^{1-\alpha}\,\pi_{\mathrm{prompted}}(\cdot\mid y_{<t})^{\alpha}. (1)

For α=1\alpha=1, the teacher recovers πprompted\pi_{\mathrm{prompted}}. For 0<α<10<\alpha<1, it interpolates toward πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}}, weakening the instruction’s influence. For α>1\alpha>1, it extrapolates beyond πprompted\pi_{\mathrm{prompted}}, strengthening the instruction’s influence. Thus, larger α\alpha corresponds to stronger instruction adherence, and CFG provides a next-token distribution at each adherence level for any instruction text, without labeled responses, external generators, or judges. The prompt format for each instruction type is given in Section B.4.

3.2 On-Policy Self-Distillation across Adherence Levels

Training across Adherence Levels. We train DIAL’s steering adapter to match the CFG teacher distributions at different adherence levels. The student παS\pi^{S}_{\alpha} is the frozen LLM with generation steered by DIAL at layer ℓ\ell. The request xx is passed to the frozen LLM, while the instruction cc and adherence level α\alpha are passed to DIAL’s steering adapter. At each prompt and generated position, the adapter replaces the residual hidden state ht∈ℝdLLMh_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{LLM}}} with an edited state ht′h^{\prime}_{t}. As in guidance distillation in diffusion models [34], a single adapter is trained to match the CFG distributions across levels.

For each request–instruction pair, we sample α∼LogUniform⁡[0.5,2]\alpha\sim\operatorname{LogUniform}[0.5,2], a distribution that is symmetric in log⁡α\log\alpha about α=1\alpha=1, where the CFG teacher recovers the prompted distribution. This range covers weaker and stronger instruction adherence than prompting. For 0.5≤α<10.5\leq\alpha<1, the teacher weakens the instruction’s influence relative to prompting, providing fine-grained intermediate training signals between unprompted and prompted generation. Beyond α=2\alpha=2, the CFG teacher’s coherence degrades (Section B.4), consistent with prior work [12]. We empirically found that sampling 24 adherence levels per instruction–request pair worked well for training DIAL across LLM families. We also verify that sampling α\alpha is important for fine-grained instruction adherence levels, and that training on more diverse instructions works better than training longer (see Section D.4).

On-Policy Self-Distillation. The student’s response distribution varies with adherence level and can differ from the prompted LLM’s. We therefore use on-policy self-distillation [45, 46], sampling student responses and computing the CFG teacher distribution at each response prefix. We minimize the Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) between teacher and student distributions per response token:

ℒ=𝔼(x,c)∼𝒟,α,y∼παS[1|y|∑tJSD(παT(⋅∣y<t),παS(⋅∣y<t))],\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}_{(x,c)\sim\mathcal{D},\,\alpha,\,y\sim\pi^{S}_{\alpha}}\!\left[\frac{1}{|y|}\sum_{t}\operatorname{JSD}\!\left(\pi^{T}_{\alpha}(\cdot\mid y_{<t}),\,\pi^{S}_{\alpha}(\cdot\mid y_{<t})\right)\right], (2)

where 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the distribution of training request–instruction pairs. Both distributions are restricted to the union of the base, prompted, and student top-64 tokens. We also add a regularization term to encourage stable training and generalization by penalizing large relative edits (Section B.4). Our loss ablation in Section D.4 suggests that JSD performs best, with forward KL performing substantially worse and reverse KL performing slightly worse. We refer to Sections B.4 and B.5 for training details and pseudocode of the full on-policy training loop across adherence levels.

3.3 Lightweight and Adaptive Classifier-Based Steering Adapter

Instruction and Memory Conditioning. We design the adapter to condition each steering edit on the instruction and the response generated so far. We encode the instruction through the frozen LLM and cache its layer-ℓ\ell hidden states ℐ\mathcal{I}. At each position, the current hidden state hth_{t} attends to ℐ\mathcal{I} and a memory of the 16 most recent edited states, ℳt={ht−16′,…,ht−1′}\mathcal{M}_{t}=\{h^{\prime}_{t-16},\dots,h^{\prime}_{t-1}\}:

zt=Attnℓ⁡(query=ht,[ℐ;ℳt]),ft=GELU⁡(LayerNorm⁡(Linear⁡(zt))).z_{t}=\operatorname{Attn}_{\ell}\!\left(\mathrm{query}=h_{t};[\mathcal{I};\mathcal{M}_{t}]\right),\qquad f_{t}=\operatorname{GELU}\!\left(\operatorname{LayerNorm}(\operatorname{Linear}(z_{t}))\right). (3)

Here, Attnℓ\operatorname{Attn}_{\ell} reuses the frozen layer’s normalization and query, key, and value projections. The current state is the query, while the instruction and memory states supply the keys and values. Since these states come from the same LLM layer, the adapter does not require a separate text encoder for the instructions. Attention combines instruction and memory states, followed by a linear map, LayerNorm, and GELU to produce the 512-dimensional feature ftf_{t}. In our experiments, a memory window of the 16 most recent states performed well while keeping attention cost low.

Adaptive Classifier-Based Steering. From ftf_{t}, the adapter predicts a unit direction ut∈ℝdLLMu_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{LLM}}}, a threshold τt​(α)∈ℝ\tau_{t}(\alpha)\in\mathbb{R}, and a norm weight λt​(α)∈[0,1]\lambda_{t}(\alpha)\in[0,1]. The direction and threshold define a linear classifier with half-space {h:⟨ut,h⟩≥τt​(α)}\{h:\langle u_{t},h\rangle\geq\tau_{t}(\alpha)\}. Unlike classifiers fitted separately for each instruction, DIAL’s classifier is generated from instruction and memory information at each token. Rather than linearly scaling a fixed steering edit, DIAL learns the threshold and norm weight as functions of α\alpha. On-policy distillation provides rich supervision from the CFG teacher for learning steering magnitude and geometry at different adherence levels.

The classifier (ut,τt​(α))(u_{t},\tau_{t}(\alpha)) determines whether and how much to steer the current hidden state. If hth_{t} lies outside the half-space, we project it onto the boundary with a minimum-norm step, following classifier-based steering [37, 38, 39]. We then adjust the projected state’s norm using the norm weight λt​(α)\lambda_{t}(\alpha) while retaining its direction. Both operations have closed-form expressions:

htP=ht+[τt​(α)−⟨ut,ht⟩]+​ut,ht′=[λt​(α)+(1−λt​(α))​∥ht∥∥htP∥]​htP,h^{P}_{t}=h_{t}+\big[\tau_{t}(\alpha)-\langle u_{t},h_{t}\rangle\big]_{+}\,u_{t},\qquad h^{\prime}_{t}=\Bigl[\lambda_{t}(\alpha)+\bigl(1-\lambda_{t}(\alpha)\bigr)\frac{\lVert h_{t}\rVert}{\lVert h^{P}_{t}\rVert}\Bigr]\,h^{P}_{t}, (4)

where [a]+=max⁡(a,0)[a]_{+}=\max(a,0). The gap [τt​(α)−⟨ut,ht⟩]+[\tau_{t}(\alpha)-\langle u_{t},h_{t}\rangle]_{+} sets the projection magnitude. Thus, the edit depends on the current state as well as the generated classifier, rather than applying a fixed steering magnitude to every token. If the state already lies inside the half-space, the edit leaves hth_{t} unchanged.

The norm weight lets the adapter interpolate between two steering geometries, which we visualize in Section B.2. At λt=1\lambda_{t}=1, the edited state is the minimum-norm projection ht′=htPh^{\prime}_{t}=h^{P}_{t} [37, 38, 39]. At λt=0\lambda_{t}=0, it preserves the original norm, ht′=∥ht∥​htP/∥htP∥h^{\prime}_{t}=\lVert h_{t}\rVert\,h^{P}_{t}/\lVert h^{P}_{t}\rVert, giving a rotation in the span of hth_{t} and utu_{t} [41, 42, 43]. Intermediate values preserve the projected direction with norm (1−λt)​∥ht∥+λt​∥htP∥(1-\lambda_{t})\lVert h_{t}\rVert+\lambda_{t}\lVert h^{P}_{t}\rVert. Learning this weight allows the geometry to adapt at each token. We found that adapters trained for different LLM families learn different norm weights and edit magnitudes, suggesting that appropriate steering magnitudes and geometries depend on the base LLM (see Section D.3). DIAL’s steering adapter has 20.6M trainable parameters on Gemma-2-9B (see Section B.1).

Efficient Inference. During inference, instruction and memory keys and values can be cached, so each token requires only a single-layer attention computation and a closed-form steering edit.

4 Experiments

We evaluate DIAL when the instruction is to express a concept, adopt a persona, or satisfy a verifiable requirement. We also compare its training and inference efficiency against baselines.

Base LLMs. We train DIAL’s adapters for instruction-tuned LLMs: Gemma-2-9B [25], Qwen2.5-7B [47], Llama-3.1-8B [48], Phi-4-14B [49], LFM2.5-1.2B [50], and Ministral-8B [51]. These cover six LLM families with 1.2–14B parameters, including Transformer and hybrid architectures.

Training Setup. We train DIAL on 14,88014,880 concept descriptions from Concept16k [19]. We also construct SteerIF, an instruction-only dataset of 98,62598,625 instructions covering concepts, personas, and verifiable and descriptive requirements, given as single or composite instructions. We train one shared adapter per LLM on SteerIF, denoted DIAL-IF. For both datasets, we remove exact and near matches to held-out evaluation instructions to assess generalization. We select a steering layer for each LLM and train its adapter at that layer. See Section B.3 for more details on dataset construction and to Section B.4 for the steered layer chosen for each LLM.

4.1 Controlling Concept Expression Levels

Training and Baselines. We train DIAL for one epoch on 14,880 concept descriptions from Concept16k [19]. We use FLAS’s released Gemma-2-9B checkpoint, trained on Concept16k with LLM-generated labeled responses [21], whereas DIAL uses only concept descriptions. We compare with prompting, per-concept methods (LoReFT, LoRA, ReFT-r1, DiffMean, and SAE [19], SV + RePS [52], and S-PSR [53]), and text-conditioned methods (HyperSteer and FLAS). We also include CFG [12, 13] for fine-grained control over concept expression, and prompting w/ level [54], which uses the same prompt as prompting but also asks the LLM to follow it at adherence level α\alpha, on a scale from 0 (ignore) to 2 (follow strongly). See Section C.1 for implementation details.

Evaluation Protocol. We evaluate on AxBench’s Concept500 (Held-In) and FLAS’s 100 held-out concepts (Held-Out). HyperSteer’s published Held-Out score uses its own held-out concepts. Neither Concept500 nor the held-out concepts appear in DIAL’s training pool. Following the AxBench protocol, we limit responses to 128 tokens and steer DIAL at layer 20 for Gemma-2-9B. Per-concept methods select a steering level for each concept, while DIAL uses a fixed adherence level α\alpha across concepts. FLAS controls concept expression through its flow time TT, with larger TT applying the learned flow for longer [21]. We use T=2T=2 as in FLAS’s reported evaluation and vary TT in Figure 3. Protocols, baselines, and further results are in Section C.1.

Evaluation Metrics. Each response receives three scores from 0 to 2: concept expression, request following (AxBench’s instruction score), and fluency. AxBench defines the overall score as the harmonic mean of the three scores. We use gpt-4o-mini [55] as a judge to compare with prior work (Table 1) and the median of three judges for the curves in Figure 3.

Concept Steering Performance. DIAL achieves overall scores of 1.059 and 1.036 on Held-In and Held-Out concepts, compared with 0.997 and 0.987 for FLAS (Table 1). Combining DIAL with prompting raises the scores to 1.198 and 1.218, compared with prompting’s 1.049 and 1.060. DIAL-IF, trained on SteerIF, steers persona and verifiable instructions and also performs well on AxBench, scoring 1.039 and 0.993.

Fine-Grained Control. DIAL’s concept score increases smoothly with the adherence level (Figure 3). From α=0.5\alpha=0.5 to 2, it rises from 0.20 to 1.42, covering a range of 1.21 points compared with 0.66 for FLAS over flow times 0.5–2. We also find that prompting w/ level does not provide fine-grained control, consistent with prior work [54]. At α=1.5\alpha=1.5, DIAL matches prompting’s concept score of 1.29 and surpasses it at α=2\alpha=2. Combining prompting with DIAL further raises concept expression, with scores from 1.35 to 1.69. The DIAL adapter thus covers intermediate expression levels below and above prompting, mirroring CFG. Although trained only on single-turn responses, DIAL also shows potential for multi-turn steering. Since an instruction given once in the context tends to lose its effect as the conversation grows [56], whereas DIAL steers the hidden state at every token during generation. Section D.5 demonstrates this advantage in multi-turn settings.

Inference Efficiency. We measure inference efficiency on Gemma-2-9B on an H200 at batch sizes of 1, 32, 128, and 256, generating 128 tokens per response. Table 2 demonstrates that DIAL retains most of the frozen LLM’s inference efficiency. In vLLM [24], it retains 96–99% of the base LLM’s throughput, compared with 41–86% for CFG and 84–86% for FLAS. Its per-token inference latency approximately matches the base LLM’s. Processing the instruction before generation increases time to first token and contributes to the remaining throughput overhead. Similar trends hold for Hugging Face. We refer to Section C.4 for absolute values and time to first token.

Training Scalability. For Gemma-2-9B in H200 GPU-hours (Table 3), DIAL uses 4.65×4.65\times fewer GPU-hours than FLAS and 25×25\times fewer than HyperSteer, with 12.4×12.4\times fewer trainable parameters than FLAS. DIAL trains using only instruction text, whereas FLAS and HyperSteer require labelled responses. With on-policy supervision across adherence levels, we found training for more than one epoch gives no consistent gain.

4.2 Controlling Persona Expression Levels

Evaluation Setup. We evaluate DIAL-IF on seven personas excluded from training, following the evaluation protocol in [57]. We compare DIAL-IF, prompting, prompt+DIAL-IF, prompting w/ level, and CFG. Three judges score persona expression from 0 to 100, and we use the median rating for each response. We refer to Section C.2 for generation, judge details, and additional results.

Fine-Grained Persona Expression. Figure 4 shows that DIAL-IF’s persona score increases with the adherence level, more linearly than CFG, using one shared adapter per LLM. On Gemma, it rises from 12.0 without instructions to 76.4 at α=1\alpha=1 and 91.4 at α=2\alpha=2, close to prompting’s 92.5. The adapter thus covers intermediate persona expression levels below, and on Qwen2.5-7B and Phi-4-14B above, prompting. Combining prompting with DIAL-IF further raises persona expression. On Qwen, the persona score rises from prompting’s 77.0 to 82.5, 84.1, and 89.6 at α=0.5\alpha=0.5, 1, and 2. On Phi-4-14B, the score rises from prompting’s 64.3 to 70.2 and 78.2 at α=0.5\alpha=0.5 and 1.

4.3 Verifiable Instruction Following

Evaluation Setup. We evaluate DIAL-IF on 541 IFEval prompts, which contain verifiable instructions on format, lexical content, and language [9]. We note that all 25 instruction types in IFEval are covered by SteerIF, though matching instruction texts are removed and 376 of its requests occur in training. The official checker assigns a binary pass/fail result to each instruction. A prompt passes only when all its instructions are followed. Unlike concept and persona expression scores, these binary checks do not measure intermediate adherence levels per response. We compare prompt-level strict accuracy at four adherence levels (α=0.5,1,1.5,2\alpha=0.5,1,1.5,2).

Instruction Following Performance. DIAL-IF alone generally improves instruction following as the adherence level increases (Table 4). On Gemma-2-9B, accuracy rises from 9.6 without instructions to 53.8 at α=2\alpha=2. At α=1\alpha=1, combining prompting with DIAL-IF improves over prompting on five of the six evaluated LLMs, while Qwen scores 71.9 compared with prompting’s 72.3. At their best levels, CFG and prompt+DIAL-IF are within two points of each other on five of the six LLMs, and CFG is higher on Phi-4-14B (72.5 against 68.2), while CFG requires two LLM passes per token. On Gemma, prompt+DIAL-IF reaches 76.9, compared with prompting’s 72.8. Llama reaches 75.6, compared with 73.6. On Phi-4-14B, LFM2.5, and Ministral-8B, it reaches 66.7, 85.6, and 65.1, versus 61.7, 83.4, and 53.4. Thus, DIAL’s adapter carries information from unseen instruction texts. We observe similar gains on the IFEval questions that do not appear in training (Section C.3).

Discussion. We differentiate instructions that apply to the whole response, such as its length or format (global), from instructions that specify particular words or positions (local). On Qwen2.5-7B, prompt+DIAL-IF at α=2\alpha=2 follows local instructions better than prompting but global instructions worse, which helps explain why its overall accuracy stays below prompting’s on this LLM (Table 4). Section C.3 covers evaluation details, category analysis, and unseen instruction types.

5 Conclusion

We introduce DIAL to build “steerable language models” that provide fine-grained control over instruction-adherence levels while keeping the LLM frozen. On-policy distillation from CFG trains a lightweight, text-conditioned steering adapter. DIAL provides fine-grained control over concept and persona expression, and combining it with prompting can improve verifiable instruction following. Training is scalable, using only instruction text and a shared adapter without labelled responses or per-instruction fitting. However, high adherence levels can still reduce response coherence, and DIAL does not improve every verifiable instruction type. Future work should explore better classifier architectures and training losses, and combine on-policy distillation with verifiable rewards or judge feedback to filter training rollouts. Future work could also explore training at negative α\alpha, matching CFG with negative weights to steer away from specific styles, topics, or vocabulary.
