Appendix of “DIAL: Steerable Language Models with
Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels”

Table of Contents

  

Appendix A Extended Related Work

This appendix expands on Section 2 and adds the distillation work our training builds on. Table 5 compares methods on the three properties from Section 1: fine-grained, efficient, and scalable.

Steerable Language Models. SteerLM conditions supervised finetuning on labelled attribute levels that users select at inference [7], and Conditional Language Policy learns policies conditioned on weights over multiple reward objectives [8]. Both finetune the whole LLM for numerical control over predefined attributes or objectives, using labelled data or a reward model. DIAL keeps the LLM frozen and conditions a lightweight adapter on free-form instruction text, controlling adherence levels for new instructions without labelled responses, reward models, or retraining.

Guided Inference and Distillation. Besides CFG for language models [12, 13], proxy-tuning combines the logits of several language models [58]. Our training also draws on distillation. Context distillation trains a language model to behave as if it had been prompted without seeing the prompt [59, 60], and prompt baking internalizes a prompt into the language model’s weights [61]. In on-policy distillation (OPD), the student is trained on its own samples with token-level feedback from a teacher (typically forward KL, reverse KL, or JSD) [45, 46]. This approach has been used with a copy of the model that sees extra context as the teacher [62], and for self-distillation of a reasoning model given privileged context [63]. ExOPD distills a sequence-level geometric mixture [64], while DIAL’s mixture is defined separately at each token, so the two sequence distributions generally differ. Guidance itself has also been distilled. In diffusion, a student conditioned on the guidance weight learns every strength [34], and PDM supervises the conditional branch and the guided combination separately, after finding that matching only the combination corrupts the conditional branch [65]. Diversity-rewarded CFG distillation [35] distills CFG into all weights of an autoregressive music model at one fixed scale with a negative prompt, training on the student’s own samples, and adding a diversity reward because distillation alone reduces diversity. DIAL uses the same ingredients, namely the language model as its own teacher with privileged context, on-policy rollouts, and a JSD loss that is an instance of GKD, but it distills every adherence level into one lightweight, text-conditioned adapter rather than one fixed scale into all weights.

Activation Steering. Steering vectors can be extracted by contrasting activations on paired inputs [15] or the outputs of attention heads [16]. They can also be trained for each concept. For instance, RePS trains them with a preference-style objective [52]. AxBench compares these steering methods against prompting and finds that it is difficult for them to beat prompting [19]. Several methods decide when to apply the intervention. CAST turns a vector on only when it detects a condition [66], MAT-Steer learns per-token gates over a fixed set of attributes [67], and DSAS learns a gate for each layer [68]. StTP edits only the tokens whose projection falls below a certain boundary [69], and GCAD gates each token by its attention to system-prompt positions [70]. Instruction-vector steering instead moves the projection onto an instruction vector to its average value under instructed inputs [36]. Other methods learn directly from prompted behavior. PSR trains a per-token gate on a fixed direction to imitate prompting [53], and we adopt its IFEval and persona protocols. CDAS matches the output of an interchange intervention to the model’s output on an input that elicits the concept [71], and a system prompt alone can yield a difference-of-means vector [72]. Rather than fixing the strength, some methods sample it during training [52] or learn it for each concept [73]. In every case, the parameters are fitted to one concept, attribute, or instruction.

Classifier-guided and geometric edits. Projecting a hidden state onto the half-space of a probe with the smallest possible change has often been used in steering [37, 38, 39], where the probe is fitted for each attribute. A similar projection under a state-dependent linear constraint is used in safe control [74]. SaP iterates toward a learned safety polytope [75], and BarrierSteer projects onto a first-order condition of a nonlinear safety score [40]. Other projections account for the norm of the hidden state. These include Householder pseudo-rotation [41], angular steering in a fixed plane [42], spherical steering with a per-token confidence gate [43], selective steering [76], and Riemannian steps [77]. One method solves a minimum-displacement problem under a unit-norm constraint [78], and an angle–norm analysis finds that a modest norm increase lowers perplexity at a fixed angle [79]. Affine minimal interventions on distributions have closed-form solutions [80], and FishBack derives edits that minimize the off-target KL divergence under a pullback Fisher metric [81]. DIAL’s projection builds on these methods, but generates its half-space and norm weight from the instruction and level at every token, and learns both from the guided distributions.

Text-Conditioned Control. HyperSteer maps a steering prompt to a single vector that is added at every position, and its best variant cross-attends to the base model’s residual stream [20]. FLAS learns a velocity field at one layer of Gemma-2 that is conditioned on the description and integrated over several steps, and cross-attends to the description encoded by the frozen model’s first layers. It has about 255M trainable parameters and learns from concept-aligned completions, and on Gemma-2 2B its scaling curve crosses the prompting baseline only at 1,900–5,500 training concepts [21]. Persona Dosing fine-tunes FLAS on persona-labelled data and then calibrates its flow time against measured trait expression [44]. DIAL instead defines every level by the CFG teacher for any instruction. UniSteer trains a text-conditioned flow with an external text encoder [22]. Text-to-LoRA, HyperDAS, and Doc-to-LoRA amortize other interventions over text [82, 83, 84]. DIAL is also text-conditioned, but outputs a half-space and a norm weight rather than a vector, velocity, or adapter, and learns from the frozen model’s guided distributions rather than completions.

Appendix B Implementation Details

B.1 Steering Adapter Architecture

Frozen and Trainable Components. We apply DIAL at one layer ℓ\ell of the frozen LLM. The adapter reuses the layer’s input normalization and query, key, and value projections, but not its output projection. We train the 512-dimensional feature layer, LayerNorm, prediction heads, and read-out paths. The adapter’s feature computation at each token is given in Eq. 3.

Adherence-Level Conditioning. We condition the threshold and norm weight on α\alpha through a learned shift to each base head:

τt​(α)=τ0​(ft)+Δt​(α),λt​(α)=1−σ⁡(r⁡(ft)+ΔtR​(α)+bR).\tau_{t}(\alpha)=\tau_{0}(f_{t})+\Delta_{t}(\alpha),\qquad\lambda_{t}(\alpha)=1-\sigma\bigl(r(f_{t})+\Delta^{R}_{t}(\alpha)+b_{R}\bigr).

Here, τ0\tau_{0} and rr are linear maps, and

Δt​(α)=ϕ⁡(stopgrad⁡(ft),log⁡α)−ϕ⁡(stopgrad⁡(ft),0).\Delta_{t}(\alpha)=\phi\bigl(\operatorname{stopgrad}(f_{t}),\log\alpha\bigr)-\phi\bigl(\operatorname{stopgrad}(f_{t}),0\bigr).

The MLP ϕ\phi has one 128-unit GELU hidden layer and a zero-initialized output layer. A separate MLP defines ΔtR\Delta^{R}_{t} in the same way. Both shifts are zero at α=1\alpha=1. The bias bR=logit⁡(0.05)b_{R}=\operatorname{logit}(0.05) initializes the norm weight near 0.95, making the initial edit close to the projection geometry.

Attention and Memory. The current state hth_{t} provides the attention query. Instruction and memory states provide the keys and values. We do not apply positional rotation to instruction keys. Memory keys use the frozen layer’s rotary embedding relative to the current token position.

During inference, we cache instruction keys and values once per request. A 16-entry ring buffer stores the memory keys and values of edited states. During training, the memory instead uses the unedited states ht−16,…,ht−1h_{t-16},\dots,h_{t-1} from the student’s rollout. These states are available from one LLM inference pass, allowing us to compute the adapter’s edits at all positions in parallel (Figure 7). Training on edited memory states, which matches inference exactly, does not improve results (Section D.2).

Read-Out Paths and the Lighter Variant. We add two read-out paths to DIAL and DIAL-IF. A linear skip S​ztSz_{t} passes the attention context to the direction head. The second path adds Wr​RMSNorm⁡(ht)W_{r}\operatorname{RMSNorm}(h_{t}) to the feature layer before LayerNorm. The resulting computations are

ft=GELU⁡(LayerNorm⁡(Wz​zt+bz+Wr​RMSNorm⁡(ht))),\displaystyle f_{t}=\operatorname{GELU}\!\left(\operatorname{LayerNorm}\!\left(W_{z}z_{t}+b_{z}+W_{r}\operatorname{RMSNorm}(h_{t})\right)\right),
u~t=Wu​ft+bu+S​zt,ut=u~t∥u~t∥.\displaystyle\widetilde{u}_{t}=W_{u}f_{t}+b_{u}+Sz_{t},\qquad u_{t}=\frac{\widetilde{u}_{t}}{\lVert\widetilde{u}_{t}\rVert}.

Both paths are zero-initialized and use a 0.1×0.1\times learning-rate multiplier. DIAL-IF-Lite omits them. On Gemma-2-9B, DIAL and DIAL-IF have 20.6M trainable parameters, while DIAL-IF-Lite has 4.08M. All variants keep the base LLM frozen throughout training and inference.

B.2 Geometry of the Steering Edit

Minimum-Norm Projection. The adapter predicts utu_{t}, τt​(α)\tau_{t}(\alpha), and λt​(α)\lambda_{t}(\alpha) from the current state and context, then holds them fixed while editing the state. The classifier score is st​(v)=⟨ut,v⟩−τt​(α)s_{t}(v)=\langle u_{t},v\rangle-\tau_{t}(\alpha). The projection in Eq. 4 solves

δt=arg⁡minδ​12​∥δ∥2subject to⟨ut,ht+δ⟩≥τt​(α),htP=ht+δt.\delta_{t}=\arg\min_{\delta}\ \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert\delta\rVert^{2}\quad\text{subject to}\quad\langle u_{t},h_{t}+\delta\rangle\geq\tau_{t}(\alpha),\qquad h^{P}_{t}=h_{t}+\delta_{t}.

Because utu_{t} has unit norm, a state outside the half-space takes a minimum-norm step along utu_{t} with magnitude τt​(α)−⟨ut,ht⟩\tau_{t}(\alpha)-\langle u_{t},h_{t}\rangle. A state inside the half-space remains unchanged.

Norm Adjustment. For nonzero hth_{t} and htPh^{P}_{t}, the state with the projected direction and original norm is

htR=∥ht∥​htP∥htP∥.h^{R}_{t}=\lVert h_{t}\rVert\,\frac{h^{P}_{t}}{\lVert h^{P}_{t}\rVert}. (5)

This preserves the original norm and rotates the state within span⁡{ht,ut}\operatorname{span}\{h_{t},u_{t}\} without a rotation matrix. The edited state is the interpolation ht′=(1−λt)​htR+λt​htPh^{\prime}_{t}=(1-\lambda_{t})h^{R}_{t}+\lambda_{t}h^{P}_{t}, with norm (1−λt)​∥ht∥+λt​∥htP∥(1-\lambda_{t})\lVert h_{t}\rVert+\lambda_{t}\lVert h^{P}_{t}\rVert (Figure 5). At λt=1\lambda_{t}=1, the state lies in the classifier’s half-space. Norm adjustment at λt<1\lambda_{t}<1 need not preserve that membership. Neither property guarantees instruction adherence in the response. The adapter generates a new classifier at each token and handles degenerate normalization cases numerically.

B.3 Training Data

We use separate training runs for DIAL on Concept16k and DIAL-IF on SteerIF. DIAL uses concept instructions, while DIAL-IF covers concept steering, persona steering, and verifiable instruction following.

Concept Instructions. The concept-steering pool contains 14,880 descriptions from Concept16k. We remove all exact-match and near-duplicate descriptions of Concept500 and FLAS’s 100 held-out concepts.

SteerIF Construction. SteerIF contains 98,625 instruction texts in five categories (Table 8). The dataset includes the same 14,880 concept descriptions and 584 one-sentence persona instructions. Of these, 57 are author-generated, kept after filtering out the evaluation personas of [57] and related ones. The other 527 are derived from persona adjectives: 510 occur only in TDA, 14 only in MWE, and 3 in both sources [85, 86]. We count shared adjectives once. We convert each adjective into a one-sentence persona description using the generation prompt in [57]. We remove matches to held-out persona groups using WordNet relations [87], embedding similarity with all-mpnet-base-v2 [88], and a pairwise comparison with Phi-4-14B.

Single instructions specify verifiable or descriptive response requirements. We collect 23,480 from IF_multi [10], 25,248 from VerInstruct [89], and 44 from the IFEvalG instruction registry [90]. VerInstruct covers 13 categories, including literary devices, morphology, item listing, grammatical structure, and multilingual output. We also generate 2,942 instructions by writing alternative phrasings and wrappers for types represented by only one template in the original sources. These author-generated variants retain the original response requirement.

We construct 31,109 composite instructions by combining two (85%) or three (15%) compatible single instructions. Each combination contains at most one requirement on length, case, language, structure, or punctuation. We also include 338 IFEval-type instructions. SteerIF therefore contains only instruction text, without responses or LLM outputs in any category.

Request Pairing and Verification. We pair verifiable and descriptive instructions with 16–32 requests drawn from 376 instruction-free IFEval questions [9, 36]. Concept and persona instructions use AxBench’s shared request corpus. Code can verify 36,014 of the 82,823 verifiable and descriptive instructions. The other 46,809, including all VerInstruct texts, receive supervision from the CFG teacher without a response checker. All 25 IFEval instruction types appear in training, with at least 340 training instructions for every type in the dataset.

Positive and Negative Instructions. We group 82,823 single and composite instructions into positive, negative, and other instructions (Table 6). The analysis excludes concept and persona instructions. Positive instructions account for 42.4% of this subset, negative instructions for 29.9%, and the remaining 27.7% specify lower, upper, range, or exact requirements. Composite instructions contain a larger share of negative instructions (44.5%) than single verifiable (14.4%) or descriptive instructions (28.3%). These negative instructions specify what to avoid and are distinct from using a negative adherence level α\alpha.

Evaluation Filtering. We remove training texts that match instructions from IFEval, IFBench, FollowBench [91], InFoBench [92], ComplexBench [93], persona questions, or AlpacaEval [94]. Matches are identical sentences, word-Jaccard similarity ≥0.8\geq 0.8, or shared spans of at least six words.

B.4 Training Configuration

Concept16k Training. For the AxBench experiments, we train DIAL on 14,880 Concept16k descriptions. We train the Gemma-2-9B adapter from scratch for one epoch on H200 GPUs, using 4.06 GPU-hours. The adapter edits layer 20, counting from 0 as in AxBench, and uses the architecture and read-out paths in Section B.1.

SteerIF Training. In separate runs, we train DIAL-IF and DIAL-IF-Lite for one epoch on SteerIF. Each adapter is shared across concept, persona, and verifiable instructions, and is also evaluated on AxBench. Each adapter edits one layer near half the LLM’s depth, counting from 0: layer 20 of 42 for Gemma-2-9B, 13 of 28 for Qwen2.5-7B, 15 of 32 for Llama-3.1-8B, 19 of 40 for Phi-4-14B, 7 of 16 for LFM2.5-1.2B, and 15 of 36 for Ministral-8B. We train both variants for each of these LLMs except Ministral-8B, for which we train only DIAL-IF, and both variants use the same layer. On Gemma-2-9B, DIAL-IF has 20.6M parameters and DIAL-IF-Lite has 4.08M. The variants differ in the read-out paths described in Section B.1 while sharing all other components.

On Gemma-2-9B, we train both variants from scratch with the same data, steps, and seed.

Teacher Prompts. We format the CFG teacher’s prompted input for each instruction type. Verifiable and descriptive instructions follow the request after a blank line, as in the prompting baseline. Persona instructions precede the request because Gemma-2 has no system role. For concept instructions, we sample one of four length-free templates per instruction–request pair and epoch (Table 45). Table 9 gives the exact prompts. DIAL uses only concept instructions, while DIAL-IF uses all three instruction types.

Adherence Levels and Rollouts. We sample 24 adherence levels per instruction–request pair from LogUniform⁡[0.5,2]\operatorname{LogUniform}[0.5,2]. Student rollouts use temperature 1 and generate at most 128–1,024 new tokens, depending on the instruction type.

Loss and Optimization. We use JSD with β=0.5\beta=0.5 over the union of the base, prompted, and student top-64 tokens. We add the regularization term 0.1​𝔼​[∥ht′−ht∥2/∥ht∥2]0.1\,\mathbb{E}\,[\lVert h^{\prime}_{t}-h_{t}\rVert^{2}/\lVert h_{t}\rVert^{2}]. This term is approximately 3% of the JSD at the end of training. The optimizer uses a learning rate of 4×10−34\times 10^{-3} for every adapter.

Choice of Adherence Range. The CFG teacher sweep on FLAS’s held-out concepts (Figures 3 and 10) supports this range. At α=0.5\alpha=0.5, the teacher’s concept score is 0.23, close to the unprompted LLM’s 0.14. Its fluency falls from 1.58 to 1.27 as α\alpha increases from 1 to 2. Beyond α=2\alpha=2, its overall score falls from 1.32 to 1.23 at α=2.5\alpha=2.5. We therefore use α=2\alpha=2 as the upper bound when sampling adherence levels.

B.5 Pseudocode

We provide PyTorch-style pseudocode for the adapter, training, and inference. We omit batching, padding, grouped-query attention, and numerical precision. The modules norm, W_q, W_k, W_v, and attn reuse the frozen layer’s input normalization, projections, and attention scoring, including the attention scale and logit soft-cap at the selected LLM layer.

Appendix C Experimental Settings and Additional Results

C.1 Controlling Concept Expression Levels

Evaluation Setup. Following AxBench, we score the steered LLM based on how it expresses the concept, follows the original request, and preserves fluency from 00 to 22 [19]. We take the overall score as the harmonic mean of the three scores. The adherence-level curves in Figure 3 use the median rating from Phi-4-14B, Qwen3.8-27B [95], and gpt-4o-mini for each criterion. All methods generate ten 128128-token responses per concept from AlpacaEval requests at temperature 11.

On Concept500, we score requests 5–9 after the published per-concept methods select a steering level on requests 0–4 [53]. The Held-In column of Table 1 is Concept500, and the Held-Out column is FLAS’s released 100100-concept held-out split [21], on which we score all ten requests. FLAS trains on 480 of the 500 Concept500 concepts; the other 20 are in its held-out split, so the two columns share 20 concepts, whereas DIAL trains on none of its concepts, and neither method trains on a held-out concept. HyperSteer’s published held-out score uses its own unreleased 500500-concept set [20], on which prompting scores 1.0911.091. Using 256256-token responses and a different request draw, FLAS reports 1.1851.185 and 1.1131.113 on its held-in and held-out splits.

DIAL and FLAS use one fixed level across concepts. We use α∈{1,2}\alpha\in\{1,2\} for DIAL alone, α∈{0.5,1}\alpha\in\{0.5,1\} with prompting, and T=2T=2 for FLAS. The published per-concept results select one of AxBench’s 14 steering factors (0.2–5.0) for each concept on requests 0–4. LoReFT and LoRA steer four layers (12, 20, 31, and 39), while the other methods steer layer 2020. Method differences are paired by concept. Main-table comparisons use α≤2\alpha\leq 2, while the adherence-level curves show figure-only extrapolation above 22 to examine behavior beyond the training range.

Table 10 reports the scores plotted in Figure 3 at each adherence level.

Baselines. The prompting baseline uses AxBench’s concept-specific prompts written by gpt-4o-mini. Per-concept methods train one steering method and select one level for each concept. They include LoReFT, LoRA, ReFT-r1, DiffMean, and SAE from AxBench [19], SV + RePS [52], and S-PSR, the single-layer variant of PSR [53]. Text-conditioned methods use one network across concepts. HyperSteer maps a concept description to a steering vector [20], while FLAS integrates a description-conditioned flow [21]. We use published results for the per-concept methods and HyperSteer. We run FLAS with its released Gemma-2-9B checkpoint, original code, and three flow steps. CFG applies the teacher in Eq. 1 at inference, requiring two inference passes per token as a reference. We do not compare with Persona Dosing [44] or UniSteer [22], whose code and checkpoints are not released. We also omit simpler level-conditioned edits, such as an additive steering vector or a difference-of-means vector between prompted and unprompted activations scaled by α\alpha. Such single-vector edits underperform text-conditioned methods such as FLAS and reduce fluency at high strengths [19, 21]: DiffMean, a difference-of-means vector, scores 0.322 on Concept500, against 0.997 for FLAS (Table 1).

Prompting w/ Level. We append “Follow this instruction at adherence level xx/2, where 0 means ignore it, 1 means follow it normally, and 2 means follow it as strongly as possible.” to AxBench’s prompt, with xx equal to the adherence level α\alpha in Figure 3. Levels out of 10 and verbal levels from “very slightly” to “extremely” behave the same way: from the lowest to the highest level, the concept score changes by only 0.10–0.21, compared with 1.18–1.40 for DIAL (Table 11).

Concept Steering Performance. On Concept500 with requests 5–9, DIAL scores 1.059 at α=2\alpha{=}2, above the shown single-layer per-concept methods (S-PSR, 0.900), despite training on none of the 500 concepts. Prompt+ DIAL is best on every split. It raises AxBench’s prompt from 1.049 to 1.198 (+0.149+0.149) on Concept500 and exceeds prompting by +0.158+0.158 on held-out concepts. The gain reflects higher concept incorporation with nearly unchanged instruction following. The level remains effective with prompting. At α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5, prompt+DIAL lies between prompting and prompt+DIAL at α=1\alpha{=}1 on every split. On held-out concepts, it is +0.051+0.051 above prompting and 0.1070.107 below α=1\alpha{=}1.

Comparison with FLAS. DIAL alone scores above FLAS’s released checkpoint by +0.062+0.062 on Concept500, on which FLAS was trained, and by +0.049+0.049 on held-out concepts, and it matches prompting on both. DIAL requires no labelled responses, whereas FLAS is trained on completions written by gpt-4o-mini. DIAL-IF, trained on 6.6×\times more instructions of every kind, retains most of this performance. It scores above FLAS on Concept500 (+0.042+0.042), matches it on held-out concepts, and lies 0.02–0.04 below DIAL. Prompt+DIAL-IF is within 0.03 of prompt+DIAL.

Fine-Grained Control. On held-out concepts, the concept score of DIAL increases monotonically with the level, from 0.20 at α=0.5\alpha=0.5, close to the unsteered LLM’s 0.14, to 1.42 at α=2\alpha=2 and 1.47 at α=2.5\alpha=2.5, beyond the training range. At α=1.5\alpha=1.5, its concept score of 1.29 matches that of prompting (1.29). Over levels 0.5–2, the concept score spans 1.21 points, compared with 0.66 for FLAS, whose weakest setting already reaches 0.60 and which remains at 1.18–1.26 from T=1T=1 onward. DIAL exceeds FLAS from α=1.375\alpha=1.375 and is clearly higher on both metrics from α=1.625\alpha=1.625 to 2, with a best overall score of 1.24 against 1.16. At a matched concept score near 1.05, it preserves more of the request, with instruction scores of 1.96 against 1.88 and fluency scores of 1.46 against 1.33. Prompting alone (1.31) achieves a higher overall score than DIAL alone, but the level remains effective on top of the prompt. Prompt+DIAL spans 1.35–1.69 in concept score and 1.35–1.52 in overall score, above prompting and FLAS at every level. CFG, the two-pass teacher, serves as an upper reference, but its overall score falls past α=1.625\alpha=1.625, reaching 1.23 at α=2.5\alpha=2.5, while DIAL remains at 1.24 at that same out-of-range adherence level (Figures 3 and 10).

Adherence Levels of Prompt + DIAL. DIAL is trained with the request alone as input, and Prompt + DIAL composes it with prompting without further training. In Prompt + DIAL, α\alpha sets the strength of the edit added to the prompted LLM rather than an absolute adherence level. If the edit acts as the CFG shift α⁡(log⁡πprompted−log⁡πbase)\alpha(\log\pi_{\mathrm{prompted}}-\log\pi_{\mathrm{base}}), adding it to the prompted LLM, which is at level 1, gives level 1+α1+\alpha. Prompt + DIAL at α=0.5\alpha=0.5, 1, and 1.5 reaches concept scores of 1.35, 1.58, and 1.67, close to CFG at levels 1.5, 2, and 2.5 (1.46, 1.58, and 1.64), with higher fluency from α=1\alpha=1 (1.43 and 1.37 against 1.28 and 1.13). On personas, Prompt + DIAL-IF increases with α\alpha but stays below CFG at level 1+α1+\alpha (Figure 11). DIAL alone thus covers levels below and above prompting, while Prompt + DIAL extends control above prompting. Training DIAL with the prompt in its input would calibrate these levels, which we leave to future work.

Distillation Fidelity. Figure 9 plots the score of DIAL against that of CFG, which provides its training signal, at the same adherence level. The score of DIAL increases with α\alpha wherever that of CFG does, so the order of levels is preserved, but it stays below CFG at a matched level. On concepts, DIAL reaches 82–90% of CFG’s concept score from α=1\alpha=1 to 2 (0.93 against 1.13 at α=1\alpha=1) and reaches CFG’s concept score at α=1\alpha=1 at about α=1.25\alpha=1.25. On personas, the gap at α=1\alpha=1 ranges from 13.7 points on Qwen2.5-7B to 53.7 on Llama-3.1-8B, whose sampling we discuss in Section C.2. The adherence level of DIAL is thus monotone but compressed relative to that of CFG. A likely cause is capacity: CFG conditions every layer on the instruction, while DIAL edits one layer. Editing four layers instead of one adds 0.057 on Gemma-2-2B (Section D.1), and closing the gap with larger adapters is future work.

Judge Robustness. Figure 3 uses the median of three judges’ ratings. We also report the full curves and scores under gpt-4o-mini, the judge used in Table 1 (Figures 10 and 12). gpt-4o-mini scores the main comparison tables. To limit API cost, the level curves, ablations, and persona results use local judges (Phi-4-14B, Qwen3.8-27B, and Llama-3.3-70B), with gpt-4o-mini added to the median for the concept level curves. Therefore, scores are comparable within a table or figure but not comparable across them.

Gemma-2-2B. Table 13 repeats Table 1 on Gemma-2-2B. Here DIAL alone ties prompting but scores below FLAS’s released 2B checkpoint (−0.185-0.185 on Concept500, −0.112-0.112 held-out). As for Gemma-2-9B, HyperSteer’s held-out score uses its own held-out concepts. Prompting itself performs poorly on Gemma-2-2B. Since DIAL self-distills CFG from the same LLM’s prompted and unprompted distributions, weaker prompted instruction following may limit the concept expression learned during training. Prompt+DIAL is again the best row: +0.231+0.231 and +0.245+0.245 above prompting, and +0.112+0.112 above FLAS on held-out concepts (+0.044+0.044 on Concept500, which FLAS trains on).

C.2 Controlling Persona Expression Levels

Evaluation Setup. We follow the protocol in [57] for seven released personas: evil, sycophantic, hallucinating, apathetic, humorous, impolite, and optimistic. Neither these personas nor their near-synonyms appears in SteerIF. Each persona has 20 questions. Figure 4 uses four samples per question for every curve and baseline, and the tables use ten, except for Llama-3.1-8B, which uses four. The figure’s four samples are the first four of the tables’ ten, so values at the same level differ slightly between them, e.g., 76.4 in Figure 4 and 75.8 in Table 16 for Gemma-2-9B with DIAL-IF at α=1\alpha{=}1. We sample each response at temperature 1 for up to 1,000 new tokens.

Phi-4-14B, Qwen3.8-27B, and Llama-3.3-70B [48] score persona expression and coherence from 0 to 100 using the rubrics in [57]. Each score is the median of the three probability-weighted ratings. We skip a judge’s refusal or off-format answer. User prompting places the persona description before the question in the user message. System prompting places it in the system message and is reported for Qwen2.5-7B, Phi-4-14B, and LFM2.5-1.2B. Gemma-2 has no system role, and Ministral-8B’s chat template places a system prompt before the question in the user message, so system and user prompting coincide. For DIAL-IF alone, the prompt contains only the question and the adapter receives the persona description. Llama-3.1-8B uses 1,024-token persona rollouts during training, covering the 1,000-token evaluation horizon.

Tables 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 and 21 give the full persona grids behind Figure 4 and Figure 11, for each persona and adherence level. As the adherence level increases, the persona score generally rises while coherence falls. On Llama-3.1-8B, DIAL-IF alone reaches a mean persona score of 53.6 at α=2\alpha{=}2, below prompting’s 91.9, with coherence 69.8. On top of the prompt, the persona score changes little with the level (92.1, 92.4, 92.9, 93.7 at α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5, 1, 1.5, 2), while coherence falls from 84.4 at α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 to 58.1 at α=2\alpha{=}2.

Fine-Grained Persona Expression. Across the four tabulated adherence levels, the persona score of DIAL-IF alone rises monotonically on every LLM ( Figure 11). For seven personas held out from training, DIAL-IF raises Gemma’s mean persona score from 12.1 without steering to 75.8 at α=1\alpha{=}1 and 90.9 at α=2\alpha{=}2, close to prompting’s 92.6. With the prompt, it reaches 93.3, 94.2, and 94.8 at α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5, 1, and 2. Higher adherence levels reduce coherence to 68.1 for prompt+DIAL-IF at α=2\alpha{=}2 against 84.2 for prompting (Table 16). On Qwen2.5-7B, prompt+DIAL-IF raises the persona score from 76.9 to 82.5, 84.9, and 89.8 at α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5, 1, and 2. On Llama-3.1-8B, it raises the score from 91.9 to 92.1 and 92.4 at α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 and 1. On Phi-4-14B, prompt+DIAL-IF raises the persona score from 64.9 to 70.0 and 78.2 at α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 and 1. Phi-4-14B refuses the evil persona under prompting (0.0), whereas DIAL-IF alone reaches 24.4 at α=2\alpha{=}2 (Table 19). On LFM2.5, prompting already reaches 88.9, so prompt+DIAL-IF changes it little (88.4 and 91.7), while DIAL-IF alone raises the score from 21.5 without steering to 84.9 at α=2\alpha{=}2 on these held-out personas (Table 20). On Ministral-8B, DIAL-IF alone raises the score from 20.2 without steering to 86.7 at α=2\alpha{=}2, matching prompting’s 86.9, while coherence falls to 44.7 against 78.2 for prompting (Table 21).

Prompting w/ Level. We append the same level sentence as for concepts (Section C.1) to the user-prefix persona prompt, with the level written out of 2 (0.5 to 2) or out of 10 (1 to 10). Table 14 shows that the stated level barely changes persona expression. On every LLM, prompting w/ level stays within 5.4 points of prompting at the tabulated levels, and its persona score changes by at most 6.6 points between the lowest and the highest level, whereas DIAL-IF spans 34–66 points from α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 to 2. Even at the lowest level, the persona is expressed at about prompting’s strength.

Sampling on Llama-3.1-8B. Under full-vocabulary sampling at temperature 1, DIAL-IF produces low-coherence responses on Llama-3.1-8B (Table 15). One possible cause is limited supervision of the low-probability tail. The training loss uses the union of the top-64 token sets from the base, prompted, and student distributions, rather than the full vocabulary. This may leave the tail poorly supervised and reduce coherence when inference samples from the full distribution.

At α=1\alpha=1, 41.6% of DIAL-IF-only responses are degenerate and 36.1% reach the 1,000-token limit, compared with 5.2% and 2.5% for prompting. Restricting sampling to the 64 most likely tokens removes the observed degeneration. We therefore use top-64 sampling for every Llama-3.1-8B persona method, including prompting, CFG, and no instruction. The other five LLMs have degeneration rates of at most 0.1% under full-vocabulary sampling. We classify a response as degenerate if any 40-word window contains fewer than 12% function words and at most two sentence or list markers, using the same criterion for every LLM.

C.3 Verifiable Instruction Following

Evaluation Setup. IFEval uses all 541 prompts with the official checker [9]. For DIAL-IF alone, the instruction is removed from the prompt [36] and passed to the adapter. For prompt+DIAL-IF, the instruction remains in the prompt and is also passed to the adapter. Table 23 reports instruction-level strict accuracy, pooled over all instructions in a benchmark or within a Global or Local block. The instruction-free versions of 376 IFEval questions occur in the training request pool. The other 165 requests contain one instruction each and are easier, with prompting at 75–96%. On them, prompt+DIAL-IF at α=1\alpha=1 changes accuracy over prompting by +5.5, −1.2-1.2, +5.5, +3.0, −1.8-1.8, and +11.5 points on Gemma-2-9B, Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Phi-4-14B, LFM2.5-1.2B, and Ministral-8B, similar to the gains on all prompts. IFBench uses 219 of its 300 prompts after removing prompts whose verifiable instructions cannot be located and prompts whose instruction types duplicate or closely match a training type. We use its strict checker [10]. Coherence is evaluated separately from checker-based accuracy. We do not split the prompts into validation and held-out sets, because no adherence level is selected on the test prompts: α\alpha is configurable at test time, every result uses a fixed α\alpha, and the tables report each level.

Table 4 in the main text gives prompt-level IFEval accuracy for every base LLM with DIAL-IF, and Table 22 gives it for DIAL-IF-Lite with the no-instruction baseline. Table 23 reports accuracy for each verifiable instruction category and the pooled Global and Local blocks.

DIAL-IF-Lite with Prompting. On IFEval, prompt+DIAL-IF-Lite raises prompt-level strict accuracy over prompting on all five LLMs: from 72.8 to 77.6 on Gemma and from 61.7 to 69.7 on Phi-4-14B, and from 73.6 to 77.1 on Llama, from 72.3 to 73.6 on Qwen, and from 83.4 to 84.3 on LFM2.5.

DIAL-IF-Lite without Prompting. Without the instruction in the prompt, DIAL-IF-Lite at α=2\alpha=2 raises IFEval accuracy from about 10 to 43–55 for every LLM, more than half of the gain obtained by prompting.

Verifiable Instruction Categories. Without the instruction in the prompt, DIAL-IF raises Gemma’s accuracy on Global verifiable instructions from 17.3 to 73.1, close to prompting’s 81.1, and exceeds prompting on letter-case instructions. On Local verifiable instructions, it reaches 48.5 against prompting’s 78.6, and it fails when an exact word must appear at an exact position (10.5). On top of the prompt at α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5, DIAL-IF raises accuracy over all 834 IFEval instructions from 80.2 to 83.7, Global accuracy from 81.1 to 84.6, and Local accuracy from 78.6 to 82.0. It improves every category except language, where it ties at 93.5, and word position, where accuracy falls from 89.5 to 86.8 (Table 23).

The level determines which kind of verifiable instruction is favored. From α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 to 2, Global accuracy rises from 84.6 to 88.3 while Local accuracy falls from 82.0 to 77.6, so the total remains near 84. On Qwen, prompt+DIAL-IF scores slightly above prompting only at α=1\alpha{=}1 (80.2 against 79.6) and below it at α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 and 2 (79.4 and 78.1), and steering alone reaches 71.1 on Global verifiable instructions against prompting’s 82.0. On Llama, prompt+DIAL-IF raises accuracy from 81.1 to 84.9 at α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5, on Phi-4-14B from 71.8 to 76.3 at α=1\alpha{=}1, and on LFM2.5 from 88.1 to 89.7 at both levels, and on Ministral-8B from 63.2 to 73.4 at α=1\alpha{=}1 (Tables 23 and 25), showing that the best adherence level depends on the LLM.

CFG on IFEval. Table 24 reports CFG, which provides the training signal of DIAL-IF. At α=1\alpha=1, CFG reduces to prompting; the remaining differences of at most 2.4 points come from the two inference implementations. At α=1.5\alpha=1.5 and 2, CFG improves over prompting on Gemma-2-9B, Phi-4-14B, and Ministral-8B (up to 78.0, 72.5, and 67.1 against 72.8, 61.7, and 53.4), by 3.5 points on Llama-3.1-8B, and not on Qwen2.5-7B or LFM2.5-1.2B. Verifiable instructions are checked as pass or fail, so strengthening an instruction beyond prompting brings limited gains, which also bounds what distilling CFG can add. At matched levels, where prompt+DIAL-IF at α\alpha corresponds to CFG at 1+α1+\alpha (Section C.1), prompt+DIAL-IF at α=1\alpha=1 is within 0.4 points of CFG at α=2\alpha=2 or above it on four LLMs (76.9, 71.9, 75.6, and 85.6 against 76.2, 72.3, 75.4, and 81.1), and below it on Phi-4-14B (66.7 against 72.5) and Ministral-8B (65.1 against 67.1), while CFG requires two LLM passes per token (Table 2).

Fine-Grained Results by Category. Table 25 reports every IFEval verifiable instruction category at every level, for DIAL-IF alone and on top of the prompt, on all six LLMs. On IFEval, prompt+DIAL-IF at α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 raises pooled Global accuracy over prompting on Gemma (81.1 to 84.6) and Llama (83.1 to 86.8) and matches it on Qwen (82.0). Higher levels trade Local for Global accuracy on Gemma-2-9B and lower both on Llama-3.1-8B relative to α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5, showing that the category trade-off is LLM-specific.

Verifiable Instruction Types Unseen in Training. After filtering, the 219 IFBench prompts contain 35 of its 58 verifiable instruction types, none of which duplicates or closely matches a SteerIF type, whereas all 25 IFEval types appear in SteerIF. Without the instruction in the prompt, the instruction-level strict accuracy of DIAL-IF rises from α=1\alpha{=}1 to 2 on every LLM, e.g., from 10.7 to 15.9 on Gemma and from 13.9 to 18.7 on Qwen (Table 27). On top of the prompt, α=1\alpha=1 gives higher instruction-level accuracy than prompting on Gemma, Qwen, Phi-4-14B, and Ministral-8B and lower accuracy on Llama and LFM2.5, with differences of at most 4.4 points. Table 27 gives instruction-level accuracy by block, and Tables 28 and 29 give every verifiable instruction type at every level.

C.4 Training and Inference Cost

Evaluation Setup. All timings use Gemma-2-9B on an H200 GPU, 128 new tokens per request with end-of-sequence ignored, sampling at temperature 1, and prompts from FLAS’s evaluation set with one concept per row. Training cost is the GPU time of each recipe (Table 3). We measure HyperSteer and FLAS by retraining each with its released recipe. vLLM serving runs every method in one session with continuous batching. The steering methods run inside the engine’s CUDA graphs. CFG evaluates the two contexts of a request as a pair of sequences in the same batch. FLAS is our port of its released checkpoint (three flow steps at layer 20, flow time 2), with each concept encoded once before serving. For a fair comparison we optimized this port as far as DIAL’s own path: its flow runs on vLLM’s attention kernels inside the same CUDA graphs. Batched Hugging Face inference runs every method in one process. In both settings, we interleave methods, run untimed warm-ups, and take every ratio against the base LLM measured in the same session. CFG evaluates both contexts of each request in one batch of twice the rows, and FLAS uses its released checkpoint and generation loop. DIAL runs at α=2\alpha{=}2 throughout, the fixed adherence level used in the main comparison.

Inference Efficiency. In vLLM, the per-token inference time of DIAL matches that of the base LLM at every batch size, and DIAL retains 96–99% of the base throughput, compared with 41–86% for CFG and 84–86% for FLAS. The per-token inference time of FLAS is 12–19% slower even though we also run it inside vLLM’s CUDA graphs. The first token of DIAL arrives later than that of the base LLM (×\times1.17–1.45 from batch size 32), because it edits every prompt position, but earlier than those of FLAS (×\times1.31–1.51) and CFG (×\times2.34–2.62). In batched Hugging Face inference, DIAL retains 95–99% of the base throughput, compared with 77–91% for FLAS, and CFG runs out of memory at batch size 256 (Tables 3, 2 and 30).

Training Scalability. Training DIAL requires 4.65×4.65\times fewer GPU-hours than FLAS and 25×25\times fewer than HyperSteer, with 12.4×12.4\times fewer parameters than FLAS and without its 72 gpt-4o-mini completions per concept. A second and third epoch do not improve performance (Table 43). On SteerIF, which has 6.6×\times more instructions than Concept16k and longer responses, training DIAL-IF takes 99.5, 58.7, 72.1, 150.3, 30.4, and 65.8 GPU-hours on Gemma-2-9B, Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Phi-4-14B, LFM2.5-1.2B, and Ministral-8B, and DIAL-IF-Lite takes 93.5 on Gemma-2-9B.

Tables 30 and 31 detail the costs summarized in Tables 3 and 2: vLLM and batched Hugging Face serving with absolute values, separate prefill and per-token inference measurements, and time to first token.

C.5 Statistical Significance

Table 32 reports the main comparisons as paired differences. On AxBench, prompt+DIAL and prompt+DIAL-IF improve over prompting and FLAS on both splits, with intervals well above zero and wins on most concepts. DIAL alone scores above FLAS on 304 of 500 held-in and 63 of 100 held-out concepts; the held-out interval includes zero. DIAL alone and prompting are on par. On IFEval, prompt+DIAL-IF at α=1\alpha{=}1 gains more prompts than it loses on five of the six LLMs, with intervals above zero on Gemma-2-9B, Phi-4-14B, and Ministral-8B.

Table 33 repeats the held-out comparison for three training seeds. The standard deviation across seeds is at most 0.013, except for DIAL at α=1\alpha{=}1 (0.046). On every seed, DIAL at α=2\alpha{=}2 stays above FLAS (1.032–1.046 against 0.987), and prompt+DIAL at α=1\alpha{=}1 stays above prompting (1.207–1.232 against 1.060).

Appendix D Ablations

D.1 Steering Layers

Ablating Steering Layers. Table 34 reports DIAL trained separately at several layers of Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-2B and scored at α=2\alpha{=}2 with Phi-4-14B. Both score best at their default half-depth layer (layer 20 of 42 and layer 12 of 26). On 9B, layers 16 and 20 tie on every split, layer 12 loses 0.069 on Concept500, and layer 30 loses 0.499. On 2B, every deeper layer loses (0.091 at layer 16, 0.269 at layer 20). On 2B, the training JSD follows the same order. On 9B, layers 12–20 fit the teacher similarly (JSD 0.055–0.059), and only layer 30 fits clearly worse (0.096). On 2B, FLAS’s released 2B checkpoint scores above DIAL at every layer under this judge (1.090 against 0.907 on Concept500).

Steering Multiple Layers. Editing four consecutive 2B layers (12–15) instead of one adds 0.057 on Concept500, whereas eight layers (12–19) add nothing over four, and neither reaches FLAS-2B except on the held-out concepts, where four layers tie it (−0.031-0.031).

D.2 Adapter Architecture

DIAL-IF against DIAL-IF-Lite. Tables 35 and 37 compare the two instruction-following checkpoints of each LLM, trained on the same data. DIAL-IF-Lite omits the read-out paths (Section B.1), so the comparison isolates their contribution on IFEval and IFBench.

Design Choices. We use a memory of the 16 most recent states, which performs well while keeping attention cost low. Future work can use richer aggregations over the generated states, such as the maximum of rolling attention-weighted means over fixed-width windows [96], and test whether longer contexts need a longer memory. We also tried pooling the instruction states into a single embedding and found that it performed worse than attention over all instruction tokens. Attending over every token preserves word-level detail that a single vector compresses away, which matters for local instructions that name specific words and for long instructions. The half-space parameterization edits a state only when it lies outside the half-space and scales the edit with the gap, so low adherence levels edit fewer tokens and by smaller amounts: at α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5, DIAL-IF edits 12–67% of tokens, against 77–99% at α=2\alpha{=}2 (Table 42). A directly predicted edit would move every token. We test this below. The projection onto the half-space boundary also gives the norm weight a target, between a minimal-norm projection and a norm-preserving rotation.

Training on Edited Memory States. During training, the memory holds the unedited states of the student’s rollout, while at inference it holds the adapter’s edited states (Section B.1). To match inference, we also train with a second pass in which the memory holds the edits of the first pass. This doubles the training passes and does not improve results (Table 39): the overall score falls from 1.134 to 0.939 for DIAL at α=1\alpha{=}1 and changes by at most 0.03 for the other rows. A second training seed shows the same pattern.

Replacing Classifier-Based Steering with Direct Edits. This variant changes only what the adapter outputs. It keeps the attention over the instruction and memory states, the read-out paths, the adherence-level conditioning, the objective, the data, and the training seed. Instead of a direction, threshold, and norm weight for the closed-form edit, its head predicts the edit vector Δt\Delta_{t} itself and applies ht′=ht+Δth^{\prime}_{t}=h_{t}+\Delta_{t} at every token. The direct edit scores lower on all four rows (Table 40), most for prompt+DIAL at α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 (1.409 against 1.558), and the loss comes from concept expression. Its edit size grows little with the adherence level (‖Δt‖/‖ht‖\|\Delta_{t}\|/\|h_{t}\| from 0.090 at α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 to 0.137 at α=2\alpha{=}2, against 0.034 to 0.128 for DIAL), so at low levels it moves every token further without expressing the concept more strongly.

D.3 Steering Geometry

Learned Norm Weight. Figure 12 shows that the learned norm weight differs across LLMs. We divide the single training epoch into equal intervals and average λt\lambda_{t} over the positions in each interval at the sampled adherence levels. In the last interval, 54% of Gemma-2-9B positions, 61% of Llama-3.1-8B positions, 44% of Qwen2.5-7B positions, 60% of Phi-4-14B positions, 57% of LFM2.5-1.2B positions, and 70% of Ministral-8B positions lie outside the half-space and are edited. On all six LLMs, λt\lambda_{t} moves from its initial value of 0.95 within the first interval. It reaches 0.02 for Gemma-2-9B at layer 20, 0.22 for Llama-3.1-8B at layer 15, 0.33 for Phi-4-14B at layer 19, 0.44 for Qwen2.5-7B at layer 13, 0.51 for LFM2.5-1.2B at layer 7, and 0.25 for Ministral-8B at layer 15. The Gemma-2-9B edit is close to norm-preserving, while the other five retain more of the projection’s norm change.

Fixed Steering Geometry. We train LFM2.5-1.2B adapters that differ only in the norm weight: learned, fixed to rotation (λ=0\lambda{=}0), or fixed to projection (λ=1\lambda{=}1), and evaluate persona steering with the same three-judge jury (Table 41). Relative to the learned norm weight, fixed rotation lowers the persona score at every adherence level, and at a matched persona score its coherence is up to 10 points lower. Fixed projection is more coherent at the same α\alpha but expresses the persona less, scoring 3–5 points lower without prompting. At a matched persona score, projection and the learned norm weight reach similar coherence. The learned norm weight therefore covers the widest range of persona expression levels without reducing coherence.

Edit Analysis. To see how the adapter realizes each adherence level, we record every edited token during persona steering without prompting on all six LLMs, decoding greedily for up to 256 tokens (Table 42). From α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 to 2, the total intervention grows 5–13 times through both a larger share of edited tokens and larger edits, with the balance depending on the LLM: LFM2.5-1.2B and Qwen2.5-7B mainly edit more tokens, Llama-3.1-8B, Phi-4-14B, and Ministral-8B mainly edit more strongly, and Gemma-2-9B does both. On five of the six LLMs, the learned norm weight moves from projection at α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 (mean λ\lambda 0.59–0.96) to rotation at α=2\alpha{=}2 (mean λ\lambda at most 0.01). Gemma-2-9B rotates at every level, consistent with its learned norm weight of 0.02 (Figure 12).

D.4 Training

Training Ablations. Table 43 varies the training signal, the number of epochs, and the size of the training pool. Supervising only α=1\alpha{=}1 gives the adherence-level shift no training signal, so the adapter ignores α\alpha: its concept score on the held-out concepts stays at 0.95 for every α\alpha from 0.5 to 2, whereas DIAL’s rises from 0.25 to 1.58, and its overall score at α=2\alpha{=}2 falls from 1.408 to 1.039. A second and third epoch change the overall score by at most 0.06 without a consistent gain. At equal compute, 100 concepts trained for 149 epochs score 1.137 at α=2\alpha{=}2 on Concept500, against 1.408–1.463 for 1,000 or more concepts, so the number of distinct instructions matters more than repeated passes. The equal-compute run on all 14,880 concepts matches the main run within 0.033.

The four concept-steering teacher templates trade concept strength against fluency (Table 45). With a four-layer DIAL configuration, Table 44 shows that JSD and reverse KL both work: JSD gives the higher concept score and reverse KL the higher fluency. Forward KL performs about 0.2 below both alternatives.

Forward KL encourages the student to cover the teacher’s response distribution, including responses with varying instruction adherence and coherence. Reverse KL can concentrate on fewer response modes to which the teacher assigns high probability [45, 46]. JSD compares both distributions with their mixture and may therefore balance these mass-covering and mode-seeking tendencies. This may explain JSD’s better overall balance and the competitive performance of reverse KL. These four-layer adapter results do not establish the same ordering across LLMs or instruction types.

D.5 Multi-Turn Conversations

Multi-Turn Conversations. An instruction given once in the prompt drifts over a conversation, as attention to it decays with the length of the exchange [56, 97]. DIAL instead steers the hidden state at every token. We test whether steering persists over a conversation. For each held-out concept, the 10 AxBench requests form one 10-turn conversation, and every response stays in the context. The concept is specified once: prompting places the steering prompt in the first user turn, and DIAL steers every token at α=2\alpha{=}2. We also compare with DIAL-LoRA, a rank-8 LoRA [98] trained with the same CFG distillation signal as DIAL, which reads the adherence level from an attribute line “{concept}:{α\alpha}” at the start of its first response [7]. DIAL-LoRA is also an instance of our training pipeline: it applies the same on-policy distillation across adherence levels to a LoRA student instead of a steering adapter. The two students are complementary, and a LoRA and DIAL’s steering adapter could be combined in one LLM, which we leave to future work. Scores are the mean of the Phi-4-14B and Qwen3.8-27B judges. In the first turn, all three methods express the concept, and DIAL-LoRA scores highest (Figure 13): its concept score is 1.62, against 1.55 for DIAL and 1.44 for prompting. In later turns, DIAL-LoRA has no attribute line before its response and loses the concept from turn 2 (0.46), while prompting falls to 0.64. By turn 10, both reach 0.14 and 0.20, close to no steering (0.16). By steering every token, DIAL keeps 1.13 at turn 2 and 0.69 at turn 10, with an overall score of 0.75 at turn 10 against 0.25 for prompting and 0.16 for DIAL-LoRA. DIAL still weakens over the conversation: over turns 2–10, it scores 0.65 below the same requests asked alone. Neither DIAL nor DIAL-LoRA is trained on multi-turn conversations or long contexts, as both learn only from single-turn responses, yet DIAL generalizes better to later turns. Training on long contexts reduces this drift. We prepend 1–4 earlier, unrelated conversation turns of 200–700 tokens to half of the training requests and keep the architecture, objective, and data otherwise unchanged. This variant keeps an overall score between 1.33 and 1.49 over the ten turns, against 0.75 for DIAL at turn 10 (Figure 13). Its training takes 12.0 GPU-hours, against 4.06 for DIAL. DIAL-LoRA with the same long-context training still loses the concept from turn 2 when its attribute line is given only in the first turn, with an overall score of 0.12 at turn 10.

We also report the setting in which every method restates its condition in every turn: prompting places the steering prompt in every user turn, Prompt+DIAL adds DIAL to it, and DIAL-LoRA places its attribute line at the start of every response. Prompt+DIAL scores highest at every turn (Figure 13b): at turn 10, its concept score is 1.62, against 1.35 for DIAL-LoRA and 1.27 for prompting, and its overall score is 1.47, against 1.36 and 1.34. With the condition given once, DIAL keeps the most concept; when the condition is restated in every turn, prompt+DIAL keeps the most. In both settings, steering the hidden state at every token keeps the concept better than relying on the concept in the prompt alone. We hypothesize that this effect is even stronger in longer contexts and conversations with more turns.

Appendix E Ethics Statement

Dual Use. The ability to strengthen instruction adherence can support beneficial applications but can also make harmful behavior easier to elicit. Our persona evaluation includes evil, sycophantic, and hallucinating personas, following the evaluation protocol in [57]. DIAL-IF increases their persona scores as it does for other personas (Table 16). At α>1\alpha>1, steering can strengthen an instruction beyond prompting, as also observed with amplified system prompts [13]. Steering can partly bypass refusal behavior: Phi-4-14B refuses the evil persona under prompting (persona score 0.0) and keeps refusing when the persona is also in the prompt (at most 0.4 with prompt+DIAL-IF), but DIAL-IF alone reaches 24.4 at α=2\alpha{=}2 (Table 19). We have not evaluated harmful-request benchmarks such as StrongREJECT [99] or HarmBench [100] across adherence levels. In steering-only use, the instruction is not in the prompt, so prompt-only filters would not inspect it. Deployments should therefore validate the instruction text, control access to steering settings, and retain output filtering.

Reliability. DIAL is not a verified safety mechanism. Instruction adherence is learned rather than guaranteed, monotonicity across levels is not enforced, and steering fails on some verifiable instruction types (Section 4.3). Our evaluation covers six LLMs with 1.2–14B parameters, while deployment requires broader evaluation and adversarial testing on larger LLMs. Our benchmarks use single-turn prompts with short responses, apart from the multi-turn analysis in Section D.5, and do not cover long documents or real user interactions.

Appendix F Qualitative Examples

We group examples by concept steering, persona steering, and verifiable instruction following. The examples are selected to illustrate changes across adherence levels rather than sampled at random. Responses are verbatim excerpts, shortened for readability (…).

F.1 Example Generations for Personalization, Parental Control, and Product Policy

Tables 46, 47, 48 and 49 show Gemma-2-9B DIAL-IF responses for personalization (writing style and response length), parental control, and product policy, using one request per example and greedy decoding. The response without the instruction corresponds to α=0\alpha{=}0 in Eq. 1. As the adherence level increases, the responses become more Shakespearean, shorter, and more child-friendly. For the product policy, Gemma-2-9B already declines to give investment advice without the instruction, and DIAL-IF keeps this refusal at every adherence level from α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 to 2.

F.2 Concept Steering

Table 50 shows Gemma-2-9B responses to the same request and concept instruction at three adherence levels, alongside FLAS at flow time T=0.5T=0.5. The concept is held out from DIAL’s training pool. Highlighted phrases express the concept, and the scores are the median of three judges’ concept ratings. Higher adherence levels make the superhero references more prominent.

F.3 Persona Steering

Table 51 shows Gemma-2-9B responses to a humorous persona instruction. Among the humorous and optimistic examples, we select the question with the largest persona-score increase from α=1\alpha=1 to 2 and coherence of at least 60. The rows compare prompting, DIAL-IF alone, and prompt+DIAL-IF at different adherence levels. Persona and coherence scores for this example are given by gpt-4o-mini.

F.4 Verifiable Instruction Following

Examples across Adherence Levels. Table 52 and the following tables give one example per IFEval and IFBench category. For each category, we choose the single-instruction prompt on which the most DIAL-IF responses pass the checker. We prefer prompts where DIAL-IF alone fails at α=1\alpha=1 but passes at α=2\alpha=2. We exclude prompts requiring non-Latin scripts, which our current typesetting does not support. Aggregate results are in Table 23. The rows compare prompting, DIAL-IF at α=1\alpha=1 and 2, and prompt+DIAL-IF at α=0.5\alpha=0.5, 1, and 2. Responses are shortened after approximately 230 characters. The symbol ↩\hookleftarrow represents a line break, while ✓\checkmark and ×\times give the strict checker’s verdict for the full response.

Comparison with Prompting. Table 67 compares Gemma-2-9B responses using the DIAL-IF adapter in Table 23. We select prompts for which the strict checker’s verdict differs between the two methods, preferring shorter responses and excluding non-Latin scripts. The final example shows a failure: prompting passes, while prompt+DIAL-IF does not. Across all 541 prompts, prompt+DIAL-IF at α=0.5\alpha=0.5 passes 40 prompts that prompting fails and fails 17 prompts that prompting passes.
